Shimōsa Nagareyama lay, as Edo saw it, in the quarter of the demon gate.
(Of all places, Toshi need not have pitched camp at Edo's demon gate.)
Kondō was no man for omens, yet on horseback from Matsudo to Nagareyama the thing oddly nagged at him.
The highway was narrow. A road barely wide enough for a single horse to pass, with dandelions blooming on either side.
"Break me off a stalk,"
he asked Chūsuke, his groom.
Chūsuke ran ahead, broke off a stalk, and handed it up to Kondō.
So yellow it stung the eyes.
Kondō held it in his mouth and rode on, swaying with the horse. The juice of the stalk seemed faintly bitter.
"Chūsuke, what do you make of this country?"
"It's a wide place, sir,"
Leading the horse by the mouth, he hunched his shoulders there in the middle of the Shimōsa plain. A wide field with no mountains is a strangely daunting thing.
Here and there in the farmland stood alder trees. If there was any variety to the scene, it was barely that.
In the town of Nagareyama there was a low rise of a hill; the place-name must have come from it.
West of the town flowed the Edo River. It was a landing-stage, too, for boats to Gyōtoku, Sekiyado, and the upper and lower reaches of the Tone.
"A town thick with mosquitoes,"
On Kondō's face, as he sat his horse, mosquitoes were swarming.

The mosquitoes were partly the doing of the water country. But above all this town was a producer of sake and mirin, with great sake warehouses everywhere through it. The mosquitoes must have bred rejoicing in the sweetness of those warehouses.
In this place Kondō dismounted from his horse before the gate of a great house known hereabouts as
"the Nagaoka sake shop"
(today the residence of Mr. Akimoto Tsuruo, sake wholesaler of Nagareyama City, Chiba Prefecture).
A billet-board hung at the entrance.
"Ōkubo Yamato, Lodging,"
it read. Toshizō must have hung it there.
Kondō passed within the gate.
Toshizō came out to meet him and showed him to a detached sitting-room.
The local headmen came to pay their respects, and when they had all taken their leave,
"Toshi, a great house, this,"
said Kondō, looking out past the thrown-open shōji.
The grounds must have run to three thousand tsubo. Within them stood a row of board-walled storehouses, several of them.
"How many storehouses are there?"
"Three. Each one runs from 150 to 300 tsubo, so they're good for quartering the men. That one across the way, it's got a mezzanine, and I've had it cleared out."
A building made to order for a barracks.
"But, Toshi,"
said Kondō, slapping a bush-mosquito on the back of his hand,
"it's a place thick with mosquitoes,"
he said wearily.
"Round here they've hung the mosquito-nets already. These are mosquitoes raised on sake, so they're twice the size of Edo's,"
and Toshizō gave his right cheek a hearty slap.
A tiny spatter of blood on the skin. Kondō, gazing intently at it,
"We've come down in the world,"
he said with a rueful smile. The Shinsengumi too were now being eaten by the bush-mosquitoes of this weed-grown riverside town.
That, no doubt, was what he found funny.
The men gathered in greater numbers than expected.
Roughly three hundred. Young men, of course, from the farming villages round about. Each was made to take a surname, given a firearm, and belted with the two swords.
Toshizō taught them all the working of the Minié rifle, and Kondō taught the methods of cut and thrust.
This district, quiet as if asleep three hundred years, grew all at once tumultuous.
Every day the crack of firing-practice was heard, and Kondō's terrific battle-cries came ringing from the "Nagaoka sake shop," so that the folk of the district feared to come near.
"Toshi, the Imperial army has Edo surrounded,"
he said — and this was on the fifteenth of the third month of the year Boshin.
The Imperial Grand Marshal's headquarters, having already pacified the post-towns of the Tōkaidō, stood at Sunpu.

Further, the Tōsandō vanguard, which had chased Kondō and the rest out of Kōshū, led by the Tosa retainer Itagaki Taisuke, reached Itabashi on the thirteenth of the third month and waited for the order to attack Edo.
The appointed day and hour for the attack on Edo had from early on been fixed for the dawn of the fifteenth of the third month.

But talks went forward between the Satsuma man Saigō Kichinosuke of the Imperial side and Katsu Kaishū of the shogunal side over the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle, and the attack was put off indefinitely.
The keeping of order in Edo was left wholly to Katsu, and the Imperial army encamped in the country round about.
One of its largest corps was the Tōsandō vanguard, with its headquarters at Itabashi.
"There are shogunal troops at Nagareyama,"
word of which came a little after the twentieth of the third month.
Spies sent to look into it found the men numbered about three hundred, all of them peasant-soldiers.
But by the dress of the commander, he seemed to be a hatamoto. The leader's name: Ōkubo Yamato.
"That'll be the same fellow we did for in Kōshū,"
said Itagaki Taisuke, the chief of staff. It was the name of a shogunal retainer that appeared in no bukan.
"Kondō, then,"
and on this reckoning they were agreed.

For this Tōsandō force, after breaking Ōkubo Yamato at Katsunuma in Kōshū, had pressed on up the Kōshū highway, entered the post-town of Hachiōji in Bushū on the eleventh of the month just past, and, making the inn Yanaseya in that town's Yokoyama-chō its headquarters under Itagaki Taisuke, carried out a search for the beaten enemy.
"This is the cradle of the Shinsengumi,"
a thing that had become common knowledge to the Imperial army.
The inquiry pressed especially hard upon the household of Satō Hikogorō, patron of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, headman of Hino post-station, and Toshizō's brother-in-law.

The family had fled at the Imperial army's coming, then scattered and moved from one relative's house to another all across the Tama country, so that their whereabouts could not easily be pinned down.
Hikogorō's son Satō Gennosuke (died Shōwa 4, aged eighty) was at this time nineteen, and had come down with scabies caught from another man's fencing gear, wasted to where he could scarcely walk.
He had fled first to relatives at Awanosu, then over the hills to the neighboring village of Utsugi, and was found hiding in the closet of a farmhouse by the Imperial search-party.
At the Hachiōji headquarters he was put to questioning.
The whole point of it was the whereabouts of his father, Satō Hikogorō. Gennosuke said he did not know.
There were three examiners; two of them spoke in so thick a Satsuma accent that he could scarcely follow. Only the third he could understand: Tani Moribe of the Tosa domain.

Tani's questioning was relentless in the extreme. Tani, the chief of staff Itagaki, all the Tosa men bore the Shinsengumi an abnormal hatred. In Kyoto many of their domain had lost their lives at the corps's hands. Above all, they believed it was the Shinsengumi who had assassinated Sakamoto Ryōma.
"Where is your father, Hikogorō?"
That was the first head of the questioning. By finding Hikogorō they meant to learn where Kondō and Toshizō were.

The second head was, "What is the relation between Hikogorō and Kondō Isami and Hijikata Toshizō?" The third: "Whether there were firearms at Hino post-station." The fourth: "The residents of Hino and the whole district round about are said once to have learned swordsmanship from Kondō Isami; how many such practitioners are there?"
They put these four points to him again and again, then shut him in a shed, and the next afternoon sat him down on a straw mat in the inner garden.

(From Gennosuke's own recollection:) The shōji before him slid open to left and right, and a man of grave and imposing bearing appeared. A guard whispered to him to bow his head. Reverently he made his salute. This personage was Itagaki Taisuke.
Itagaki, seeing that Gennosuke was a sick man, did not question him much. Only,
"Is it true that Ōkubo Yamato and Naitō Hayato, on setting out to the field, took their noon meal at your house and gave audience to the local men?"
he said.
The same question had been put to him the day before. That time it had been phrased, "Kondō, Hijikata —"
Today Itagaki used, offhandedly, the names "Ōkubo, Naitō." Gennosuke, drawn in before he knew it, answered, "That is so."
By this the Imperial army knew who the owner of these aliases was.
And he, they learned, was encamped at Nagareyama.
At the Imperial headquarters in Itabashi there was a stir of excitement. Had this Tōsandō vanguard not had Tosa men for its main strength, perhaps it would not have seethed so.
"Let us take our revenge for Kyoto,"
such was the fever that filled the camp.
On the Imperial side, holding the rank of deputy staff officer and charged with the office of standard-bearer,
was a man named Kagawa Keizō.

Originally a Mito retainer, he had been posted to the Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto and kept up a busy traffic with the extremist loyalists of Chōshū and Tosa; before long he deserted his domain and threw in with the Rikuentai, the rōnin corps of the Tosa domain.
The captain of the Rikuentai was Nakaoka Shintarō, who met a violent death together with Sakamoto Ryōma, captain of the Kaientai.

After Nakaoka's death the command of the corps passed to the Tosa deserter Tanaka Kensuke (later Mitsuaki, count), and Kagawa became its vice-commander; at the time of the Battle of Toba-Fushimi they encamped on Mount Kōya as a detached force of the anti-shogunal army, holding the Kishū domain in check.
After the Restoration Kagawa held one court office after another, ending as Grand Master of the Empress Dowager's Household, a count, and dying in Taishō 4 at the age of seventy-seven.

He had the nickname "Kagawa the Fox," and there was something sly and dark in his nature; even Tanaka Mitsuaki, his comrade of long standing from the last days of the shogunate, fell out with him after the Restoration, and Tanaka would not so much as speak to him until Kagawa died.
This Kagawa,
"I ask to be added to the force that will wipe out the Shinsengumi. It is to repay what is owed for Nakaoka,"
he petitioned at the Itabashi headquarters. As a request it was reasonable enough.
But this man, with his splayed bald crown and his round staring eyes, was no hand at commanding a corps.
It was settled that the Satsuma man Arima Tōta (a deputy staff officer, later Sumio) should lead three hundred men to the subjugation, and Kagawa went along attached to the force.
Arima's force left its billet at Senju at the dawn of the second of the fourth month.
Arima knew that spies from Nagareyama were slipping constantly into the neighborhood of Senju.
So, to deceive his own troops, he told the men,
"We march for Koga,"
and that night stayed at Senju, and the next day put up at Kasukabe (today the city of Kasukabe).
The next morning he suddenly turned his force about, marched south, and came before long to the west bank of the Tone.
When the startled men asked him why, Arima pointed across to Nagareyama on the far bank,
"We attack that,"
he said.
Gathering at once every boat to be had from the farmhouses and fishing-houses nearby, they crossed the river with lightning speed and massed below the embankment.
It was morning, about nine o'clock.
The first in the Nagareyama settlement to see what was afoot were a few soldiers on guard to the west of the town.
They opened fire at once.
But the range fell short, and the Imperial side, moreover, stayed perfectly still and did not fire back so much as one shot.
"Toshi, that's gunfire,"
said Kondō, and as he did a lookout came running in to say the enemy had attacked.
"Right, I'll go and see,"
and Toshizō ran to the stable, mounted, and, riding this way and that through the narrow lanes of the settlement, came out at the western edge of the town.
(So it is.)
Far off, in the shadow of the houses by the embankment, the shapes of the Imperial troops kept appearing and vanishing.
Five hundred figures, he reckoned, and, thinking it better to strike first himself, galloped back to headquarters.
"Everyone, gather in the yard of the main camp,"
he shouted.
He reached in from the edge of the veranda and slid open the shōji of Kondō's room.
"What is it?"
Toshizō was startled.
Kondō had changed into plain clothes.
"Toshi, I'm going over to the Imperial camp. To explain that we are not men who would raise a hand against the brocade banner,"
"Are you in your right mind?"
"I am. These last few days I've thought it through. It seems this is about the crest of the pass,"
"The crest of what pass?"
Kondō did not answer. He knew that to answer would start an argument.
Kondō put on straw sandals with white thongs.
"If I talk to them, they'll understand,"
Kondō was making light of the Imperial army. It never crossed his mind that the true identity of Kondō Isami, commander of the Shinsengumi, had already been found out.
He had only to plead that the force mustered at Nagareyama was stationed there, in short, to keep order on the east bank of the Tone.
Should the Imperial army say this would not do, he need only disband them; he did not think it would take any harder line than that.
For as to the keeping of order within Edo itself, the Imperial army half-sanctioned the Shōgitai and had, in effect, left the matter to them.
(Was the Nagareyama muster not the same?)
So Kondō made light of it.
"Don't,"
said Toshizō.
"It's like walking into a trap,"
"No, it'll be all right. And besides, Toshi,"
said Kondō.
"For a long time I've deferred to your judgment. But this once, let it be as I will,"
Kondō was smiling. It was a smile more at peace than any Toshizō had ever seen on him.
"I'll be back directly,"
Kondō went out the gate, taking two of his men.
A single rice-paddy path ran all the way to the farmhouse the Imperial troops had made their post.
Kondō let the two men lead, and walked slowly, treading the grass.
Before long he came before the farmhouse with its brushwood fence. When an Imperial soldier leveled his rifle to bar the way,
"I come as an envoy,"
he said, staying him, and asked to see the commander.
Presently he was shown into a sitting-room.
"I am Ōkubo Yamato,"
said Kondō.
Arima, with the soft manner of a Satsuma man, asked his business.
Beside him was Kagawa Keizō.
Neither Arima nor Kagawa knew Kondō's face by sight. But of his singular features they had heard.
(No mistake — it was the man.)
Kagawa's eyes glinted with a cold blue light.
"As to this morning's affair,"
said Kondō,
"my men, not realizing you were the Imperial army, fired carelessly. I have come to apologize,"
"That was ill done. You may have your reasons, but in any case your explanation, troublesome as it is, must be made at the headquarters in Kasukabe. And your firearms are to be handed over at once,"
"Understood,"
nodded Kondō. What was in his heart at that moment, Toshizō could not know.
"Let me return to camp first, and then,"
and with that Kondō came back.
Toshizō argued furiously.

In the end he wept. Don't, give it up, there is still Ōshū — again and again Toshizō roared it at him. At the last he went so far as to fling it in his face: on the way up you're fine, but the moment the road turns downhill you throw everything away, like a man made over.
"That's so,"
Kondō nodded.
"I don't want to leave the name of a rebel behind me. Unlike you, I understand the great cause and the rightful name,"
"'Loyalist' and 'rebel' are things of a moment. But for a man, is surrender not a thing to be ashamed of? Go back to being the man you were when you spoke of going to seize a million koku in Kōshū,"
"The time has passed, Toshi. It has gone by, clean over our heads. Kondō Isami, Hijikata Toshizō — both of us have become orphans of an old age,"
"No,"
Toshizō fixed his eyes on him. The tide of the times was beside the point. Victory or defeat, out of the question. A man ought to die for the beauty he holds in his own mind, said Toshizō.

But Kondō said quietly: I feel the beauty in bowing to the great cause. Toshi, comrades a long time we've been, but at the very last it seems our views have split, over what it is we each find beautiful.
"And so, Toshi,"
said Kondō.
"You go your road. I'll go mine. Let us part here,"
"I won't part. I'll take you with me,"
Toshizō seized Kondō's sword-arm. It was as sturdy as the low bough of a pine.
He half thought Kondō would shake the hand off and fling it away, but instead, unexpectedly, Kondō stroked it.
"You've done much for me,"
"Hey —"

"Toshi, set me free. You built the Shinsengumi into an organization. You made me, too, the head of that organization. The Kondō Isami who was in Kyoto — looking back now, I feel that was not really me. Loose me now; set me free,"
Toshizō looked into Kondō's face.
He stood dumbstruck.
"I'm going,"
Kondō stepped down into the garden. Down, and straight off to the sake warehouse, where he ordered the men to disband, then gathered the few corpsmen who had been with him since Kyoto,
"Let every one of you go free. I too will be free. You've all done much for me,"
Kondō went out the gate once more.
Toshizō did not follow.
(I go on fighting.)
He gave his face a slap — smack. A bush-mosquito, its legs jet-black, lay crushed there.
